title: Chips, power and water
essentialQuestion: What does AI need from the planet, and who pays for it?
learningGoal: Explain what AI data centres need from the planet, where they are built in Southeast Asia, and how governments weigh their benefits and costs.

warmUp.question: When you ask an AI tool a question, where do you think the answer is made?
options: In a big building far away

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each person hope for? What does each person worry about?

cards.title: A data centre is coming to Coralton

cases.name: The data centre company
cases.body: “We will build a huge building full of computers that run AI tools. About 1,000 people will help to build it over two years. About 50 people will work there after it opens, and we will train local young people for some of those jobs. We will put solar panels on the roof.”

cases.name: Hana, who runs a small fish farm
cases.body: “My fish need clean water and power all day and all night. I worry that the data centre will use the town's water in the dry season, and that power cuts will get longer.”

cases.name: Leo, a young electrician
cases.body: “I hope to get work on the building site and learn new skills. Two years of work would help me a lot.”

cases.name: The town's water office
cases.body: “In the dry season, the river is low. The data centre needs water to cool its computers. It could use cleaned waste water instead of river water.”

cases.name: A member of the town council
cases.body: “The company will bring money to Coralton. But most people who use its AI tools live in other countries.”

sections.heading: Where an AI answer is made
sections.text: When you ask an AI tool a question, your device usually doesn't make the answer itself. Some small tools can run on a phone or laptop. But most of the time, the question travels to a data centre, a large building full of computers. Its chips do huge numbers of sums each second. They use a lot of electricity and get very hot, so many data centres use water to cool them. The International Energy Agency estimated that in 2024, all the world's data centres used about 1.5% of its electricity. It thinks about 15% of that was for AI. The rest was for other work. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages. The agency expects data centres to use about twice as much by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast, not a measurement, and the agency says it is uncertain.
sections.simpler: Usually, an AI answer is not made in your device. Some small tools do work on a phone. But most questions go to a data centre. This is a big building full of computers. Its chips do huge amounts of maths. They use a lot of power and get very hot. Water often helps to cool them. In 2024, all data centres used about 1.5% of the world's power. Only a small part was for AI. Data centres also run videos and messages. Experts think the power they use may double by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast. It is a guess, not a fact yet.

sections.heading: Chips need minerals and a few factories
sections.text: Chips are made from materials dug out of the ground. Some need rare minerals, which are often mined in ways that harm nature. Very few factories can make the most powerful chips. A 2021 chip industry study found that 92% of the most advanced chips were made in Taiwan. So a problem in one place could slow chip supplies around the world. Old chips and computers also become electronic waste, which can contain harmful metals such as mercury and lead.
sections.simpler: Chips are made from things dug out of the ground. Some need rare minerals. Digging them up can harm nature. Only a few factories make the best chips. In 2021, a study found most are made in Taiwan. A problem there could slow chips everywhere. Old computers become waste. Some of it is harmful.

sections.heading: Singapore, Johor and Batam make choices
sections.text: Data centres need land, power and water. So where they go is a choice for governments. By the early 2020s, data centres used about 7% of Singapore's electricity. Singapore paused new ones in 2019. From 2022, it let in only a few that met strict rules on saving energy. Many companies built across the border in Johor, in Malaysia, and on Batam, in Indonesia. In the first ten months of 2024, Malaysia drew more than 31 billion US dollars of investment in data centres. The energy agency expects data centres to cause as much as a fifth of the growth in Malaysia's power use by 2030. Building them brings work that ends when the building is finished. Running them brings some long-term jobs. These often need special training. Some experts say data centres bring far fewer jobs than they promise. People nearby worry about water and power cuts. In November 2025, Johor stopped saying yes to the most basic kinds of data centres. These can use far more water. The rules are still changing.
sections.simpler: Data centres need land, power and water. So governments choose where they go. Singapore paused new data centres in 2019. They used a lot of its power. From 2022, it let in only a few that saved energy. So many companies built in Johor, Malaysia, and Batam, Indonesia. They brought a lot of investment. Building them gives work for a few years. Running them gives some long-term jobs. Some experts say there are fewer jobs than promised. People who live near them worry about water and power cuts. In 2025, Johor stopped saying yes to some data centres that use lots of water. These rules keep changing.

glossary.definition: A large building full of computers that store and process information.
glossary.example: The new data centre in Coralton will run AI tools.

glossary.definition: A tiny part inside a computer that does its sums.
glossary.example: The data centre has thousands of chips, and they get very hot.

glossary.definition: A careful guess about the future, based on evidence.
glossary.example: The 2030 number is a forecast, not a measurement.

glossary.definition: A natural material that people dig out of the ground.
Money a company spends in a place, hoping to earn more later.
glossary.example: The data centre is a big investment in Coralton.

checks.question: The energy agency says data centres may use twice as much power by 2030. What kind of number is this?

options.text: A measurement of what already happened
options.feedback: Not quite. 2030 hasn't happened yet. Read the end of the first section.
Yes. It is the agency's careful guess, and it says the guess is uncertain.

options.text: The power used by AI alone
options.feedback: Not quite. It is for all data centres, which also run videos and messages. Read the first section.

checks.question: What happens to the building work at a data centre?

options.text: It lasts as long as the data centre runs
options.feedback: Not quite. Building work is for building it. Read the third section.

options.text: It is done by computers, not people
options.feedback: Not quite. People build data centres. Read the third section.

options.text: It ends when the building is finished
options.feedback: Yes. Building work lasts a few years. After that, there are some long-term jobs inside.

write.prompt: Should Coralton say yes to the data centre? Give your answer, one benefit, one cost, and one promise you would ask the company to make.
sentenceStarters: I would ask the company to promise ...
write.example: I think Coralton should say yes, but only with a promise. One benefit is that about 1,000 people get building work for two years, and people like Leo can learn new skills. One cost is that the data centre needs a lot of water to cool its chips. In the dry season, Hana's fish farm and the town's homes could get less. I would ask the company to promise to use cleaned waste water, not river water. Johor made rules about water too.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner is Hana, the fish farmer, and says one worry about the data centre. You are the data centre company, and you answer with one promise. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud the difference between building jobs and long-term jobs at a data centre. Then say why the difference matters to a town.

watch.title: Why are AI data centers using so much electricity? - Sajan Saini
watch.why: A short animated lesson shows what is inside an AI data centre, why it gets so hot, and asks how much of the planet's resources AI should use.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think is inside an AI data centre?
watch.afterQuestion: What two ways does the video give to make AI use less energy?
watch.summary: This animated lesson explains why AI data centres use so much power. The video says that since 2019, more than a thousand huge AI data centres have been built. It says each one can use as much water as a small town, and as much power as a small city. Inside are thousands of computers with special chips. The chips do trillions of sums each second. All this work makes them very hot. Engineers cool them with water or special liquids. They also send data with light, which wastes less power. But AI tools keep getting bigger, so they need more and more power. The video asks if we could build smaller tools for smaller jobs. It ends with a question: how much of the planet should we use for smarter machines?
keyPoints: AI data centres use huge amounts of electricity and water.
Chips get very hot, so engineers look for new ways to cool them and save power.
People must decide how much of the planet's resources AI should use.
watch.contentNote: About 6 minutes (6:16), an animated TED-Ed lesson by Sajan Saini, released in September 2026, with fast American English. The title and channel were confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 31 October 2026, and the length is from TED's page for the lesson. The summary was written from the transcript on TED's website (https://www.ted.com/talks/sajan_saini_why_are_ai_data_centers_using_so_much_electricity), not from watching it. It names two AI tools (Claude and ChatGPT), uses US examples (New York City), and mentions companies planning their own nuclear power plants. Its numbers (for example, enough energy for 300,000 homes) are the video's own and are not repeated in the lesson. Someone on the team must watch it before use; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Power cuts, water shortages and the cost of electricity may be part of learners' daily lives. Don't ask about their homes, bills or access to water and power; keep the discussion on Coralton and the reported facts. Some learners may live in or near the places named (Johor, Batam, Singapore): keep it neutral, about choices every town faces, not blame for any country or its people.
educatorNotes: The numbers are dated and scoped. Electricity: the International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report (April 2025) estimated that all data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity; AI servers were about 15% of data-centre electricity (24% of server electricity) that year. It projects about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses now, with AI the main driver and with stated uncertainty (the pace of AI use, efficiency gains, bottlenecks). These figures were read in Scientific American (10 April 2025) and AFP via The Star (10 April 2025); the IEA's own pages refused access on 8 November 2026, so check them if you can. At the launch, the IEA's head said data centres were on course to account for “as much as one-fifth” of Malaysia's electricity-demand growth to 2030 (a projection, not a measurement; reported by Hydrocarbon Engineering and GreenTechLead). On the device: some small models run on phones and laptops (for example Apple's roughly 3-billion-parameter model, 2024), while most large tools run in data centres. Taiwan's 92% of the most advanced chip-making is from a 2021 Semiconductor Industry Association study (Reuters, 1 April 2021). Minerals and e-waste (mercury, lead) are from UNEP (21 September 2024). UNEP's “800 kg of materials for a 2 kg computer” (no source given) stays out.

Singapore, Johor and Batam: Singapore paused new data centres in 2019; reports put their share of its electricity at about 7% (AP dates it to 2019, Kontinentalist to 2021, DatacenterDynamics in 2022 says over 7%). From 2022 a pilot call admitted a few new ones that met strict efficiency rules (a PUE below 1.3, top green-building certification); about 80 MW went to four operators, and a 2024 Green Data Centre Roadmap promised at least 300 MW more. Johor grew from nearly nothing in 2019 to at least 1.6 GW planned (AP, February 2025), and Malaysia drew over US$31 billion of data-centre investment in the first 10 months of 2024 (Knight Frank, via AP). Jobs: building work ends when the building is finished; a typical data centre has 30 to 50 permanent jobs and large ones up to 200, according to Good Jobs First, a US group (via AP and an ISEAS commentary, March 2025). That figure is not measured for Johor, so it is not in the learner text. In November 2025 Johor stopped approving Tier 1 and Tier 2 data centres, which can use up to 200 times more water than higher tiers; in February 2026 Malaysia's prime minister said approvals for new non-AI data centres had been limited. Rules change quickly: check the latest before teaching the third section. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages, not only AI. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW06.md.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: both readings now say the answer is usually made in a data centre and that some small tools run on the device; the 1.5% is described as all data centres in 2024 (the IEA's 2025 report), with only part of it for AI, and the 2030 doubling as a forecast; building work (temporary) is separated from long-term jobs; the unsourced “most give only 30 to 50 jobs” (and its quick check) and UNEP's unsourced 800 kg figure were removed; Singapore's 7% is now dated 2021; Malaysia's hopes and the investment are added as local benefits, and Coralton's company now trains local young people (a new activity item replaces Hana's power-cut item, which the electricity item covers). Coralton stays fictional and labelled; real sources are in the reading and teacher notes, not mixed into the evidence. Activity feedback gives reasons without “Most people would say” and accepts other groups where a reason fits. Six sources (one over the checker's aim) because the on-device point needed its own. Claim record: claims/DW06.md.

Revised on 8 November 2026 from Justin's brief of 4 November: the Benefit-or-cost sort, the think question, the planning boxes and the self-check were removed. The reading now separates all data-centre electricity (about 1.5% in 2024) from AI's share (about 15% of it), marks the 2030 figure as an uncertain forecast (new glossary word and quick check), and teaches the regional decisions: Singapore's 2019 pause and 2022 efficiency rules, the move to Johor and Batam, Malaysia's 2024 investment and the IEA's projection that data centres may cause as much as a fifth of its electricity-demand growth, building versus long-term jobs, and Johor's November 2025 water rule. The 800 kg and “30 to 50 jobs” figures stay out of learner text (the jobs figure is in the teacher notes with its US scope). The visual is now a map.
